Business Combination Accounting The operating results of Cox Communications have been included in the Company's consolidated statements of operations for the period from the date of acquisition through September 30, 2026. For the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, revenues attributable to Cox Communications since the acquisition date were $ 1.4 billion. Certain Cox Communications’ operations have already been integrated with the Company’s existing operations, including shared functions and infrastructure. Because these costs cannot be attributed to Cox Communications without assumptions and allocations that would not provide a meaningful measure of its results, it is impracticable to determine its earnings since the acquisition date. Charter applied business combination accounting to the Cox Transactions. The purchase price was allocated to the identifiable assets acquired and liabilities assumed based on their estimated fair values, with the excess recorded as goodwill. Fair values were preliminarily determined using income, cost and market approaches, primarily based on third-party valuations using management’s assumptions, including expected future cash flows. These inputs are largely unobservable (Level 3), except for assumed long-term debt and the Charter Holdings common units, which were valued using quoted market prices (Level 1). Property, plant and equipment was valued using the cost approach, which considers replacement cost adjusted for physical depreciation and functional and economic obsolescence. Franchise rights and customer relationships were valued using a multi-period excess earnings method, a discounted cash flow approach that isolates the cash flows attributable to each intangible asset. The weighted average life of customer relationships acquired is 7 years. Deferred tax assets and liabilities were recorded for acquisition-date differences between book basis and tax basis, subject to the transaction structure. The Contribution was treated as a nontaxable partnership contribution, and no deferred taxes were recorded in purchase accounting as the basis difference in the partnership from the net assets contributed was associated with Cox Equity Holdings. The Equity Sale was treated as a taxable stock acquisition and the tax attributes of the Cox Communications’ subsidiaries were carried over to Charter and net deferred tax liabilities of $ 438 million were recorded in purchase accounting reflecting book versus tax temporary differences of these subsidiaries applying Charter’s effective tax rate. At closing, Charter, Cox Equity Holdings and A/N entered into an amended tax receivables agreement, which sets forth the terms pursuant to which Charter will pay each of Cox Equity Holdings and A/N 50 % of tax benefits arising from future exchanges of their common and preferred units. No tax sharing liability to Cox Equity Holdings was recorded for this contingent consideration obligation in purchase accounting since the tax benefit is dependent on uncertain future events that are outside Charter’s control. A future exchange is not based on a fixed and determinable date and the exchange is not certain to occur. The Charter Holdings common units issued to Cox Equity Holdings, which are exchangeable into Charter Class A common stock, were measured at fair value based on the closing price of Charter Class A common stock on the acquisition date. These difficulties include: • integrating the companies’ operations and corporate functions; • integrating the companies’ technologies, networks and customer service platforms; • integrating and unifying the product offerings and services available to customers; • harmonizing the companies’ operating practices, employee development and compensation programs, internal controls and other policies, procedures and processes; • maintaining existing relationships and agreements with customers, providers, programmers and other vendors and avoiding delays in entering into new agreements with prospective customers, providers and vendors; • addressing possible differences in business backgrounds, corporate cultures and management philosophies; • consolidating the companies’ administrative and information technology infrastructure; • coordinating programming and marketing efforts; • coordinating geographically dispersed organizations; • integrating information, purchasing, provisioning, accounting, finance, sales, billing, payroll, reporting and regulatory compliance systems; 38 • integrating and unifying the product offerings and services available to customers, including customer premise equipment and video user interfaces; • managing a larger company than before the completion of the transactions; and • attracting and retaining the necessary personnel associated with the acquired assets. Even if the new businesses are successfully integrated, it may not be possible to realize the benefits that are expected to result from the Cox Transactions, or realize these benefits within the time frame that is expected. For example, the elimination of duplicative costs may not be possible or may take longer than anticipated, or the benefits from the Cox Transactions may be offset by costs incurred or delays in integrating the businesses and increased operating costs. If the combined company fails to realize the anticipated benefits from the Cox Transactions, its liquidity, results of operations, financial condition and/or share price may be adversely affected. In addition, at times, the attention of certain members of our management and resources may be focused on the integration of the businesses and diverted from day-to-day business operations, which may disrupt our business.
